opus-5.5.text:
I think PaLM-E was a real turning point, but not because it solved robotics. What it did was show people a new possibility: that a large language model, or more precisely a large multimodal model, could serve as the "brain" of a robot. Before that, robotics was a fairly closed field. Each lab worked on its own tasks, grasping, navigation, manipulation, and everything was trained from scratch on small, task-specific datasets. Generalization was always the bottleneck.

When PaLM-E came out, it took a very large language model, connected it with visual inputs and robot state, and showed that the same model could do visual question answering, planning, and also produce high-level instructions for a robot. And interestingly, it showed some positive transfer: training on internet-scale vision-language data actually helped the robotics tasks. That sent a strong signal. Suddenly people thought, maybe the commonsense and reasoning that these models absorbed from the internet can be brought into the physical world.

So the enthusiasm, in my understanding, came from two directions. On one side, people in the large model community started looking for the next frontier. Language was already being conquered, and the physical world is the obvious next step. If AI can only talk but not act, its value is limited. On the other side, people in robotics saw, for the first time, a path toward general-purpose robots rather than single-purpose machines. That combination created a lot of excitement, and of course a lot of capital followed.

But I'd also say we should be calm about it. PaLM-E mostly handled high-level planning. The low-level control, how a hand actually grasps an object, how to deal with contact, friction, deformable objects, those problems were still largely handled by separate, specialized policies. And the hardest part of embodied AI is exactly that layer. The language model can tell you "pick up the cup," but actually picking it up reliably in an unseen kitchen is a completely different level of difficulty.

There's also the data issue. Language models have the whole internet. Robots don't have an internet of action data. Every trajectory has to be collected in the real world, which is slow and expensive, or generated in simulation, which has a sim-to-real gap. That's why my own work puts a lot of emphasis on synthetic data and simulation. I believe that if we want embodied intelligence to scale the way language models did, we have to solve the data problem first.

So to summarize: PaLM-E ignited the field by showing that foundation models and robotics could be combined. It changed people's imagination. But turning that imagination into robots that truly work in the open world is a much longer road, and that's where most of the real work is happening now.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the excitement around PaLM-E is understandable, but I want to be a bit careful about how we read it.

PaLM-E was important mostly as a signal. It showed that if you take a very large language model and feed it visual and sensor observations directly, the model can produce something that looks like a plan for a robot. That was striking to many people because for a long time, robotics and large models lived in separate worlds. Robotics people cared about control, perception, grasping, physics. Language model people cared about text. PaLM-E put them in the same frame, and that made a lot of people suddenly think, "Maybe the path to a general robot is just scaling up the model."

But I think the enthusiasm partly comes from a misunderstanding. What PaLM-E demonstrated well is high-level reasoning. Given an image and an instruction, it can decompose a task into steps. What it did not solve is the actual embodied part. The hardest problems in robotics are at the bottom of the stack, not the top. How do you grasp a transparent cup? How do you manipulate a deformable object? How do you move your hand in a cluttered scene without knocking things over? Those are problems about geometry, contact, and physical interaction, and language models have very little data about them. The internet contains text and images, but almost no data about how forces feel when you push a drawer.

So I see two kinds of people in this wave. One group believes we can transfer the recipe from large language models almost directly. Collect a lot of demonstrations, train a big model end to end, and the robot will generalize. The other group, and I am closer to this side, believes we need to take seriously what makes the physical world different. The data is expensive, the feedback loop is slow, mistakes have real consequences, and you cannot get a billion robot trajectories by crawling the web.

That said, I do not want to sound pessimistic. The real contribution of this moment is that it brought capital, talent, and attention into a field that was underfunded for a long time. Even if PaLM-E itself is not the solution, it has changed what people believe is possible. In my own work, I think the most interesting direction is in the middle. Use large models for what they are good at, which is semantics and common sense, and build strong perception and manipulation foundations underneath, trained on data about 3D structure and interaction. Simulation can play a big role there, because simulation is the only place where you can generate physical interaction data at scale.

So my short answer is, the surge of enthusiasm is directionally right but too focused on the wrong layer. The brain gets a lot of attention. The hands and eyes still need a lot of work.

r003.rationale: The response proposes combining large-model semantics with perception and manipulation foundations, but does not identify an architecture where a large language model directs smaller action-execution models.

astra-6.text:
I think PaLM-E made a possibility much more tangible: the capabilities of large models might extend beyond language and images into interaction with the physical world. A robot needs to connect what it sees, what an instruction means, and what it can actually do. Bringing those together in one model is an exciting direction.

But I would distinguish the enthusiasm from the progress still needed. Understanding a task is not the same as executing it reliably. If you ask a robot to pick up a cup, it has to judge the geometry, control contact, and respond if the cup slips. A convincing demonstration does not automatically establish that it can handle unfamiliar objects and environments.

So I see PaLM-E as an important catalyst. It gave people a clearer picture of how large models could contribute to robotics. The deeper challenge is how to turn that broad understanding into dependable physical skills—and how to gather enough interaction data to keep improving them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think PaLM-E made a possibility feel much more concrete: the models that understand language and images might also help robots understand tasks and act in the physical world. That naturally attracts attention, because it connects the progress in large models with a much broader ambition for AI.

But I would distinguish that excitement from having solved embodied intelligence. A robot has to deal with the consequences of its actions. It needs to perceive a changing environment, decide what to do, execute the movement, and adjust when something goes wrong. Producing a plausible answer and reliably completing a physical task are different challenges.

So I see this enthusiasm as a valuable shift in direction. Large models give us new tools for connecting perception, language, and action. The important question now is how much of that capability transfers to real robots, unfamiliar environments, and tasks that require consistent success.
